              A Counting Lemma for Somewhat Restricted 3-APs
               Amey Bhangale*               Subhash Khot†              Yang P. Liu‡           Dor Minzer§

                                                         Abstract
           For a prime p ⩾ 3, a somewhat restricted 3-AP in Fnp is a triplet (x, x + a, x + 2a), where x ∈ Fnp
       and a ∈ {0, 1, 2}n . We prove a counting lemma for somewhat restricted 3-APs in dense sets in Fnp .
       More precisely, we prove that for all α > 0, there exists β > 0, such that for sufficiently large n, if a set
       A ⊆ Fnp has density at least α, then it contains at least β fraction of all somewhat restricted 3-APs.
           Our proof builds on recently developed machinery from [Bhangale, Khot, Minzer, 2026]. Our main
       new ingredient is an arithmetic regularity lemma for patterns such as somewhat restricted 3-APs. This
       result is in the spirit of arithmetic regularity lemmas from the theory of Gowers uniformity norms [Green,
       Tao, 2010] and may be of independent interest.


1    Introduction
The emergence of arithmetic patterns in dense sets, first studied by Roth [Rot53], has proven to be a fun-
damental problem relating distinct areas in mathematics. Roth’s theorem asserts that for all ε > 0, if
A ⊆ {1, . . . , N } has density at least ε and N is sufficiently large, then A must contain a triplet of the form
x, x+a, x+2a with a ̸= 0. Variants and extensions of Roth’s theorem have received much attention over the
years, and their study led to the development of important tools in combinatorics, analysis, ergodic theory,
probability and more. Below are a few of these results:
    1. Quantitative bounds: the precise density needed for the conclusion to hold has been the subject of in-
       tense study [Bou99, Bou08, San11, BS19, BS20, KM23]. By now, it is known that the answer is quasi-
       polynomial [KM23, BS23], matching the shape of the best known construction [Beh46, EHPS24].

    2. Longer progressions: Szemerédi’s [Sze75] extended Roth’s theorem to progressions of arbitrarily
       large constant length. Further study of this problem led to the development of higher-order Fourier
       analysis [Gow98, Gow01] and of graph and hypergraph regularity [Sze78, RS78, Gow07].

    3. More general patterns: the study of arithmetic progressions has motivated the broader question
       of the occurrence of general patterns in sufficiently dense sets. A concrete class of examples are
       polynomial progressions [BL96], which are patterns of the form x + P1 (a), . . . , x + Pk (a) where
       P1 , . . . , Pk are polynomials. Other examples include multi-dimensional patterns [FK78, Gow07]
       (such as x + ia1 + ja2 for i, j = 0, 1, 2), and combinatorial lines [FK91, Pol12, BKLM25].

1.1     The Finite Field Setting
In the finite field setting, one considers the problem of finding arithmetic patterns in a dense set A ⊆ Fnp .
Here and throughout, p is thought of as a prime of constant size and n is thought of as tending to infinity.
The theory in this setting is very close to the theory in the integer setting, and it avoids some of the technical
difficulties (such as dealing with Bohr sets). In fact, the tools in the two settings are close analogs of one
another, with the exception of the polynomial method [CLP17, EG17], which only seems applicable for
some problems in the finite field setting.
     Meshulam [Mes95] proved an analog of Roth’s theorem in the finite field setting, following a similar
density increment, Fourier-analytic strategy. Our work is mostly concerned with studying more restricted
patterns than the ones addressed in Meshulam’s work, defined as follows:

Definition 1.1. Fix a prime p ⩾ 3.

   1. A somewhat restricted 3-AP in Fnp is a triplet of the form (x, x + a, x + 2a) such that x ∈ Fnp and
      a ∈ {0, 1, 2}n \ {⃗0}.

   2. A restricted 3-AP in Fnp is a triplet of the form (x, x+a, x+2a) such that x ∈ Fnp and a ∈ {0, 1}n \{⃗0}.

      One may consider two distinct problems with respect to restricted 3-APs and somewhat restricted 3-APs:

   1. Existence: what density guarantees that A must contain at least one pattern?

   2. Counting: if A has density α > 0, does it have to contain Ωα (1) fraction the patterns (provided n is
      sufficiently large)?

The Fourier analytic machinery employed by Meshulam [Mes95] and subsequent works does not seem to
apply well to this setting, and these problems were highlighted in [Gre25, HHM18]. For the first problem,
the density Hales Jewett theorem implies that any constant density must contain at least one pattern. The
quantitative bounds this argument gives were quite weak, and only recently effective bounds were given.
For both problems, it is now known [BKM24a, BKLM25] that if A ⊆ Fnp contains no restricted 3-AP, then
it has density at most 1/(log log log n)cp where cp > 0 is a constant. As far as we know it may be the case
that A must have exponentially small measure, and a recent result [CFP26] shows this is indeed the case for
the richer class of progressions of the form (x, x + a, x + 2a) where a ∈ {0, 1 . . . , (p + 1)/2}n .

   1. The single function setting: suppose that we have a single collection of product functions P, which
      we want to “process” into a high-rank collection. Intuitively, a violation to the high-rank condition
      means that there is a non-trivial dependency between functions in P. If this dependency took a very
      simple form, such as being able to express P1 ∈ P as a product of other P ∈ P, then one could move
      to a smaller collection P ′ ⊆ P in a way such that T1−ε,P ≈ T1−ε,P ′ . 2 Indeed, we show that there is

       values CP . In particular, it allows one to give strong estimates of their probabilities, show strong
       mixing results on random walks starting in them, and so on.
